source: Murre & Dros (2015) Replication and analysis of Ebbinghaus' forgetting curve
finding: One-subject replication of Ebbinghaus 1885. Same shape, but savings lower at every delay. No 24-hour boost found.
limits: N=1. 10 lists per delay. 31-day lists learned early, so confounded with practice and fatigue. Table 2 and Table 3 disagree.
agent_relevance: Forgetting is steep early and flattens. A power-law-like decay is a safe shape, but the constants differ a lot by person and material.

source: Murre & Dros (2015) curve fits
finding: Power function and summed exponentials both fit well. The sum of exponentials fit slightly better but not meaningfully by AIC.
numbers: Dros: power R2=0.974, AIC=-16.6; summed exponential (Memory Chain Model) R2=0.995, AIC=-24.5. Mean over four datasets: power R2=0.987, AIC=-22; summed exp R2=0.996, AIC=-23.5. AIC gap of 2 is the cut-off for meaningful.
limits: Savings measure, nonsense syllables, one new subject. Seven delay points only, so few degrees of freedom.
agent_relevance: Power law is not uniquely favoured by data. The ACT-R decay form is a convenient choice, not a proven one. Do not over-tune d.

source: Rivera-Lares, Logie, Baddeley & Della Sala (2022) Rate of forgetting is independent of initial degree of learning
finding: Four experiments replicate Slamecka & McElree 1983: extra repetitions raise starting recall but do not change the rate of forgetting.
numbers: Exp1 N=60 (2/4/6 reps; 30s, 24h, 1wk); Exp2 N=60; Exp3 N=60 Spanish (30s, 24h, 3d); Exp4 N=40. Exps 2-4 no substantial reps x delay interaction. Exp1 three interactions, put down to floor at 1 week.
limits: About 20 per cell. Floor effects at 1 week. Custom sentences. Remote testing by email or phone. Bayesian mixed models report credible intervals, not Bayes factors.
agent_relevance: ACT-R with per-trace decay tied to activation (Pavlik & Anderson 2005) predicts stronger items decay faster. This data says strength does not change the slope. Use use-count to raise rank, not to change decay speed.

source: Cohen-Dallal, Fradkin & Pertzov (2018) Are stronger memories forgotten more slowly?
finding: Stronger visual short-term memories were not forgotten more slowly. No strength x delay interaction in three experiments.
numbers: N=22, 21, 21. Interaction Bayes factors favouring no interaction: 5.47/7.31/6.29 (non-informative prior); pooled 11.86 (non-informative) and 9.54 (informed). Delays 1 s and 6 s.
limits: Visual orientation memory, only two short delays. Not the same system as ACT-R declarative memory. Result depends on error measure scaling.
agent_relevance: Same direction as b03 from a different system. Weak support that strength and decay rate are separate.

source: Stocco, Rice, Thomson, Smith, Morrison & Lebiere (2023) ACT-R declarative memory and its neurobiology
finding: Current statement of the declarative equations: A = B + S, power-law base level, spreading W/N, partial matching, blending. Pavlik-Anderson variant gives each trace its own decay, set by activation at creation and a rate parameter alpha.
numbers: Cited correlates: Zhou et al. 2021, N=50, alpha correlated with resting EEG power; Hake et al. 2023, alpha separated amnestic patients from controls at over 80% accuracy (N not stated in text). Retrieval odds equal 1 when B=0.
limits: Self-described as speculative. No new data. ACT-R has no encoding interference, no episodic/semantic split, no active forgetting.
agent_relevance: Lists what ACT-R leaves out: encoding interference and active forgetting. A memory ranker built from ACT-R inherits those gaps.

source: Autry & Levine (2014) A fan effect in anaphor processing: effects of multiple distractors
finding: Five experiments: more same-category nouns in a list slow and degrade retrieval of the referent. Distractor probes suffer more.
numbers: Exp1A N=85, 15.2 ms/noun; Exp1B N=54, 31.3 ms/noun; Exp2A N=69; Exp2B N=50, accuracy for distractors 0.92 to 0.72 (2 vs 5 nouns); pooled F(1,265)=15.56, d=0.24 (95% CI 0.12-0.36).
limits: Pooled effect is small. Many effects significant by items only. Exp 3 anaphor effect not significant. Reading times fell with list length, against the prediction. Heavy exclusions. Cannot split storage from retrieval interference.
agent_relevance: Fan effect is real but small in sentence tasks. When many memories share one cue, each is diluted, so keep overlapping facts few or split by cue.

source: Pirolli (2016) A computational cognitive model of self-efficacy and daily adherence in mHealth
finding: ACT-R base-level equation fit to a 28-day mHealth adherence study. Fitted decay was near the upper bound of 1.
numbers: Data: Konrad et al. 2015, N=65 (19 adaptive, 24 easy-fixed, 22 difficult-fixed). Math model d=0.9394, 95% CI [0.1204, 1]. RMSE 0.083 (ACT-R simulation) and 0.060 (math model).
limits: Fit to the same data it is scored on. CIs hit bounds. No baseline. ACT-R parameters not systematically explored. Single study.
agent_relevance: Decay on a day scale is not the lab default d=0.5. Parameters must be refit for the timescale of the agent's memories.

source: Pirolli, Mohan, Venkatakrishnan, Nelson, Silva & Springer (2017) Implementation intention and reminder effects (JMIR)
finding: Reminders raised daily goal success. Spaced reminders beat massed ones at high frequency, as a power-law activation model predicts.
numbers: N=64, 28 days. Daily success: high-freq distributed 0.55, high-freq massed 0.38, low-freq massed 0.34, low-freq distributed 0.32, none 0.18. Reminders vs none OR=7.52, P<.001. Frequency x distribution interaction OR=2.22, chi2(1)=13.06. In-sample Brier 0.1724.
limits: Cells of 11-14. Interaction power 0.22-0.59; effect may be overstated about 1.56x. Self-report. In-sample fit only. Model predicts a more sublinear recency effect than seen. Base-level parameters differ from lab values.
agent_relevance: Spacing helped only at high frequency, not low. Refresh important memories at spaced times, but expect no gain when refreshes are rare.

source: Kangasraasio, Jokinen, Oulasvirta, Howes & Kaski (2019) Parameter inference for computational cognitive models with ABC
finding: Fitting an ACT-R model with four methods gave the same retrieval threshold and latency factor but different noise and base-level constant. Those two are weakly identified.
numbers: Estimates (RT/ANS/LF/BLC): grid -3.0/0.06/0.07/14.3; Nelder-Mead -2.9/0.03/0.070/16.9; Bayes opt -2.9/0.001/0.07/6.9; ABC -2.9/0.08/0.07/12.2. Automatic fit cut prediction error by 16% against hand-tuned values.
limits: Aggregate data only; N not stated; train equals test, so overfitting untested. Model could not reproduce difficulty level 3. Skill-acquisition model, not pure declarative recall.
agent_relevance: Do not trust a hand-set noise or offset in a ranker. Only threshold and speed constants were stable across fitting methods.

source: van der Velde, Sense, Borst, van Maanen & van Rijn (2022) Capturing dynamic performance in a cognitive model: LBA for ACT-R memory parameters
finding: Latency factor and activation means are hard to separate; noise and non-decision time recover best. A week of retrieval practice by army recruits changed activation over sessions.
numbers: Simulation: 25 simulated people, 25 to 50,000 trials; recovery reasonable at 100 trials, plateau near 250. Empirical: 50 of 127 recruits kept, 12,568 of 29,441 trials. Accuracy rose session 1 to 2 (z=-4.68, p<.001), flat 2 to 3 (p=.8).
limits: Retrieval failures lumped with wrong retrievals; threshold not modelled; empirical session effects exploratory; a speed march between sessions 2 and 3.
agent_relevance: Parameter trade-offs mean several settings fit equally well. Prefer few free parameters in the agent's memory score.

source: Anderson & Schooler (1991) Reflections of the environment in memory
finding: Founding rational analysis: the chance a memory is needed follows a power-law shape in newspaper headlines, child-directed speech and email, as human forgetting does.
numbers: Not opened this session. Exact figures not recorded here.
limits: Environmental statistics from three corpora; the link from need probability to human retention is argued, not tested at the individual level. Recalled from background knowledge.
agent_relevance: Grounds the rank-by-recency-and-frequency rule in a statistical argument, not only a fit.

source: Averell & Heathcote (2011) The form of the forgetting curve and the fate of memories
finding: Rival-form test: compared power, exponential and other forgetting functions on retention data, including individual-participant fits. Result not verified here.
numbers: Not opened (publisher page returned 403). 192 citations per Crossref.
limits: Not verified. Check before building any claim on power law vs exponential.
agent_relevance: Open this one before any claim about the form of the forgetting curve.

source: Murre & Chessa (2011) Power laws from individual differences in learning and forgetting
finding: Rival explanation: a power-law average can arise from a mixture of exponential decays with different rates across items or people. Recalled, not verified here.
numbers: Not opened (Springer redirect). 48 citations per Crossref.
limits: Not verified.
agent_relevance: If true, a single power law per memory is the wrong unit; a mix of fast and slow traces fits as well.

source: Park, O'Brien, Cai, Morris, Liang & Bernstein (2023) Generative Agents
finding: Retrieval score is a normalised sum of recency, importance and relevance. Recency is exponential decay with factor 0.995 since last access. Removing memory, planning and reflection lowered rated believability.
numbers: Recency decay 0.995; relevance = cosine similarity; all weights 1. 100 Prolific raters ranked five conditions. TrueSkill: full 29.89, no reflection 26.88, no reflection or planning 25.64, human crowdworker 22.95, no memory/planning/reflection 21.21. Kruskal-Wallis H(4)=150.29, p<0.001; d=8.16 full vs prior-work baseline.
limits: The ablation removes whole modules, not only the recency term. Rater believability, not recall accuracy. Time since last access resets on retrieval, unlike ACT-R's full history sum.
agent_relevance: The most used agent memory rank. It uses last-access recency only, not frequency. A full-history sum is untested here.

source: Hou, Tamoto & Miyashita (2024) 'My agent understands me better' (CHI EA)
finding: Dialogue agent whose recall probability rises with relevance and recall count and decays with elapsed time through a modified sigmoid. Beat the Generative Agents score on a small recall task.
numbers: 10 tasks drawn from chat histories; loss lower than Generative Agents, t=-5.687, p=0.000299, 95% CI of mean difference [-0.27,-0.12], critical t=2.26. Six participants rated dialogue qualitatively.
limits: Ten tasks only; tasks built from the authors' own system chat logs; both models failed Task 0. Loss is mean squared error on softmaxed scores. No ACT-R mention.
agent_relevance: Adding recall frequency helped on repeated-habit questions but failed on one-off events.

source: Hou, Tamoto & Miyashita (2024) Task 0 failure analysis
finding: Both Hou's model and Generative Agents failed when the user announced a one-off concert on a usual day. Frequency pulled Hou's model to the habit; recency and relevance pulled Generative Agents to the latest event.
numbers: Task 0 of 10: both models incorrect.
limits: Single case. Authors' own error analysis.
agent_relevance: A history-of-use score is a prior about habit. A novel event needs another path, such as an explicit override.

source: Zhong et al. (2023) MemoryBank
finding: Memory strength rises by 1 on each recall and decays by an Ebbinghaus exponential R=e^(-t/S); retrieval by dense similarity. Evaluated with human-labelled probing questions for SiliconFriend.
numbers: Labels: memory retrieval 0/1, correctness 0/0.5/1, contextual coherence 0/0.5/1. No ablation of the forgetting term found in the text read.
limits: Exponential, not power law; forgetting term not isolated in an ablation. Strength increment of +1 is a design choice.
agent_relevance: Shows decay is widely used in agent memory; gives no measured benefit of the decay itself.

source: Hou, Tamoto, Zhao & Miyashita (2025) SynapticRAG
finding: Adds temporal association, spike propagation and a leaky integrate-and-fire cutoff to retrieval. Each module's removal cost accuracy against the full system.
numbers: Four datasets (English, Japanese, Chinese). Gain over RAG up to +14.66 points (avg 10.41). Ablations, mean change: no temporal integration -9.90, no stimulus propagation -4.35, fixed time constant -10.54. ERC-MG accuracy 86.21%; PerLTQA-CN 93.12%.
limits: Dialogue sets built for temporal questions. Baseline strength varies by dataset. Not an ACT-R test.
agent_relevance: Time-aware scoring beats similarity-only on time-spread chat. The dynamic time constant mattered most.

source: Synapse (2026) Empowering LLM agents with episodic-semantic memory via spreading activation
finding: Spreading activation with fan-out division, temporal decay and lateral inhibition on a memory graph beat other agent-memory systems on LoCoMo. Removing node decay or activation dynamics cost the most.
numbers: LoCoMo, GPT-4o-mini. Average F1 (no adversarial): Synapse 40.5, Zep 39.7, MemoryOS 38.0, LangMem 34.3, A-Mem 33.3, MemGPT 28.0. Ablation F1: no node decay 30.7 (temporal 50.1 to 14.2), no activation 30.5, no fan effect 36.1, vectors only 25.2. About 814 tokens/query vs 16,910.
limits: Margin over Zep is only 0.8 F1. LLM-judge scoring. Fan penalty and decay are tuned (rho=0.01, S=0.8). Cold start weak. Lateral inhibition can hide minor details. Headline +7.2 is against A-Mem.
agent_relevance: Best LLM-side evidence that ACT-R-style spreading, fan and decay each add accuracy. Decay mattered most on temporal questions.

source: Meghdadi, Duff & Demberg (2026) Embedding cosine similarity in ACT-R spreading activation
finding: Replaced ACT-R's hand-coded similarities with Word2Vec or BERT cosine. Added to frequency and visual terms it improved fit to lexical decision times; a fan penalty gave a further small gain.
numbers: Semantic Priming Project, about 6,631 pairs, 512 participants. Spearman rho: frequency only 0.42; plus visual 0.48; plus CoSim Word2Vec 0.50 (p<0.01 vs B3); plus fan 0.51 (p=0.02). CoSim alone rho 0.20-0.21. Regression benchmark 0.51, RMSE 65.16 ms vs best model 75.97 ms.
limits: Matches a plain regression, does not beat it. Association strength grid-searched on test data. No test against the original hand-coded values. Noise set to zero. One 200 ms SOA.
agent_relevance: Embedding cosine is a usable stand-in for ACT-R similarity, but alone it is weak (rho 0.2); frequency does most of the work.

source: Innerebner, Kowald, Schedl & Lex (2025) Hybrid personalization using ACT-R declarative and procedural modules
finding: Vision paper for recommenders: base-level activation plus context spreading plus production-rule boosts. No experiments.
numbers: None: no dataset, N, or parameter values.
limits: Untested proposal.
agent_relevance: Do not count as evidence. Shows interest, not results.

source: Latimer et al. (2025) Hindsight is 20/20
finding: Not ACT-R. Four-network memory with retain, recall, reflect. A strong non-activation comparison on LongMemEval and LoCoMo (abstract only).
numbers: Abstract: 20B model 39% to 83.6% over full-context; 91.4% LongMemEval and 89.61% LoCoMo with a larger backbone; best prior open LoCoMo 75.78%.
limits: Abstract only; no decay term tested.
agent_relevance: Structured memory with reflection can beat decay-based ranking; do not assume activation is needed.

source: Settles & Meeder (2016) A trainable spaced repetition model (half-life regression)
finding: Fit forgetting by regressing half-life on features, on 12.9 million Duolingo traces. Cut error against the Leitner rule and logistic regression; dropping the half-life term hurt a lot. Not an LLM, but the largest memory-decay test found.
numbers: MAE: HLR 0.128; HLR without half-life term 0.350; Leitner 0.235; Pimsleur 0.445; LR 0.211; constant 0.175. AUC all near 0.51-0.54. Live test HLR-lex vs HLR: +12.0, +1.7, +9.5 (%) on retention measures, 3.3M students, p<0.001. Authors note ACT-R is power-law and HLR exponential.
limits: AUC near chance (0.538 for HLR), so item ranking is weak though calibration is good. Lexeme features failed to help much.
agent_relevance: Modelling decay explicitly cuts calibration error roughly in half versus a fixed schedule; ranking individual items stays hard.

source: Yao et al. CoALA (2023) Cognitive architectures for language agents
finding: Framework paper: places retrieval from episodic memory by recency, importance and relevance. No ACT-R-style decay tested.
numbers: No experiments on retrieval ranking.
limits: Conceptual only.
agent_relevance: Do not count as evidence for decay; it only names the design space.

source: A3-Bench (2026) Benchmarking memory-driven scientific reasoning via anchor and attractor activation
finding: Not ACT-R. Supplying the right activated memory (concepts and solution templates) raised accuracy of ten LLMs on science problems, most on the hardest.
numbers: Average accuracy across ten LLMs 34.71% to 48.19% (+13.48) with annotated activation; anchor-and-attractor paradigm +11.12 over vanilla and +6.35 over CoT; physics competition Qwen3-4B 1.69% to 7.63%.
limits: Annotated activation is an oracle upper bound, not a retrieval method; gain depends on getting the right memory.
agent_relevance: Upper bound: if ranking surfaces the right template, gains can be large. Ranking quality limits it.
